overview: This file consists of three Department of State “List of Papers” index sheets summarizing and cross-referencing records on Japan’s iron and steel industry from 1930 to 1939. The entries cover the proposed Showa Steel Works at Anshan, industrial rationalization, consolidation of government and private mills into the Japan Iron Manufacturing Company, metallic minerals and ferro-alloys, zinc-smelting pollution, the role of imported scrap, and American involvement in transferring a steel-machinery plant from Wooster, Ohio, to Japan. Later entries also record concern about American contracts for Japanese plants capable of manufacturing steel rails, armor plate, and other potentially strategic materials; the underlying reports, memoranda, correspondence, and clipping are referenced but are not reproduced in the surviving pages.

subfiles.title: List of Papers entries 17–18: Showa Steel Works and industrial rationalization
subfiles.about: Indexes two 1930 reports from Japan concerning the proposed Showa Steel Works at Anshan and efforts to rationalize Japan’s steel industry.
subfiles.summary: Entry 17 refers to Neville’s July 1, 1930 report on a planned Showa Steel Works at Anshan, organized as a collateral company of the South Manchuria Railway Company with capital of ¥100 million and a stated annual capacity of 500,000 tons. Entry 18 refers to his August 1 report on a July 23 meeting of advisers to the Department of Commerce and Industry’s Temporary Industrial Rationalization Bureau. Copies were reportedly attached, while the originals were filed under 894.00 P.R./31 and /32.

subfiles.title: List of Papers entries 20–27: steel consolidation, industry statistics, and the Wooster plant
subfiles.about: Indexes records on consolidation of Japan’s steel industry, metallurgical production and pollution, scrap supplies, and a proposed American transfer of steel-making machinery to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references Grew’s reports on legislation consolidating government mills with five large private companies and subsequent criticism of the proposed Japan Iron Manufacturing Company. It also lists a Tokyo report on zinc smelting and sulphur fumes, a Military Attaché report on metallic minerals, iron and steel, and ferro-alloys, and State Department memoranda on the importance of scrap iron and steel to Japanese industrial development. The remaining entries concern political discussions and interdepartmental correspondence over the purchase of the idle Mackintosh-Hemphill plant at Wooster, Ohio, by the United Engineering and Foundry Company for shipment to Japan and possible joint manufacture of steel-making machinery.

subfiles.title: List of Papers continuation: Wooster factory transfer and armaments-related industrial contracts
subfiles.about: Indexes September–October correspondence and reports concerning transfer of the Wooster steel factory and American contracts for industrial plants in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The first entries record Marian Spence’s request for information about the transfer of the Wooster factory and the shipment of war materials to Japan, together with its referral to the Commerce Department. A Division of Controls memorandum by Green reports Charles F. O. Arensberg’s decision to accept contracts to supply machinery for Japanese plants manufacturing paints, steel rails, and armor plate, following referral through the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce and a telephone conversation. The final entry identifies an October 13 report by Helen Loomis of the China Information Service on the Wooster factory transfer.

interest: The index is useful as a compact map of otherwise dispersed State Department records on Japan’s prewar metallurgical expansion. It links domestic consolidation, Manchurian heavy industry, dependence on imported scrap, pollution, and military-relevant production to specific diplomatic, military, congressional, and commercial records. Especially noteworthy is the trail documenting American participation in transferring machinery and expertise to Japan for making steel-production equipment, rails, and armor plate shortly before the Second World War.
